procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 14, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court, Lucknow Bench in Criminal Appeal No. 425 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court convicted six people and acquitted one. The convicted persons appealed to the High Court, and their appeal failed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Subedar, one of the convicted persons, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The respondent (State) argued that the Supreme Court should not interfere with the conclusions of the two lower courts. The Supreme Court disagreed, stating that it can interfere under Article 136 if there has been a grave miscarriage of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by two lower courts.

facts: The appellant was found guilty by two lower courts (the trial court and the High Court).
On appeal to the Supreme Court, the respondent's counsel argued that the Court should not interfere with these concurrent findings of guilt.
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has a wide, overriding, and exceptional power to hear appeals.
The general rule is that the Supreme Court does not normally review or reappraise evidence in criminal cases, especially with concurrent findings from lower courts.
However, this power is to be exercised sparingly and in the furtherance of justice.
An exception to the general rule exists: the Court is not only empowered but expected to interfere when a judgment has resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice.
A grave miscarriage of justice can occur due to a misapprehension or mistake in reading evidence, or by ignoring material evidence.
application: The Court disagreed with the respondent's contention that it should not interfere.
It found that the exception to the general rule applied in this case.

The Court determined that the lower courts had caused a grave miscarriage of justice by ignoring a previous Supreme Court warning regarding cases based on circumstantial evidence, specifically the danger of allowing conjectures and suspicions to take the place of proof.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it should interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt. It held that while it does not normally do so, it is empowered and expected to intervene under Article 136 when the lower courts' judgment results in a grave miscarriage of justice, as it did in this case by improperly handling circumstantial evidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 136 of the Constitution, should interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by two lower courts.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the Supreme Court should interfere because the lower courts' judgments resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice by misapprehending or making a mistake in reading the evidence, or by ignoring material evidence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent contended that the Supreme Court should not interfere with the concurrent conclusions of the two lower courts that held the appellant guilty, especially on a special leave appeal under Article 136.

cases.case_name: Hanumant v. The State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, there is a danger of conjectures and suspicions taking the place of proof. The evidence must necessarily point only to the guilt of the accused, excluding any reasonable possibility of his innocence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which a conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established, and the established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt. The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature, excluding every hypothesis except the one to be proved, and the chain of evidence must be so complete as to leave no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.
obiter: The Supreme Court, under Article 136, is empowered and expected to interfere with lower court findings, even on matters of evidence, if the judgment has resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice due to a misapprehension or mistake in reading evidence or by ignoring material evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a case based solely on circumstantial evidence, the lower courts caused a grave miscarriage of justice by ignoring the established legal warning against allowing conjectures and suspicions to replace proof. The evidence presented did not satisfy the test that circumstantial evidence must point exclusively to the guilt of the accused, excluding any reasonable possibility of innocence, which warrants the Supreme Court's interference under Article 136 to set aside the conviction.
legal_tests_applied: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent findings of fact under Article 136 when the judgment under appeal has resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice by some misapprehension or mistake in the reading of evidence or by ignoring material evidence.

In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with the guilt of the accused, be of a conclusive nature, and exclude every hypothesis except the one to be proved. The chain of evidence must be so complete as to leave no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.
policy_considerations: The power conferred by Article 136 is worded in very wide terms and is not hedged in by any technical hurdles.
This over-riding and exceptional power has been vested in the Supreme Court to be exercised sparingly and only in furtherance of the cause of justice.
